en.title: Social Work: the whole course
en.short: What social work is, how social work degrees are organised, the main areas, and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Social work is a practice-based profession and an academic discipline. It helps people, families, groups and communities to improve their wellbeing, cope with hardship and change unjust conditions. Social workers assess needs and strengths, plan interventions, act, and review results. They work in child protection, health, mental health, schools, community development, welfare administration and many other settings.

The subject draws on sociology, psychology, law, social policy, economics and research. It is not only kindness or charity. In many countries social work is regulated, with protected titles, codes of ethics and continuing professional development. Its core values include human dignity, social justice, self-determination, confidentiality and professional boundaries. Practice must respect human rights and the law of the country concerned.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degrees differ by country and institution. Common patterns are a three-year or four-year bachelor’s degree, a one-year or two-year master’s, and supervised fieldwork in every professional programme. In Nigeria, universities offer the Bachelor of Social Work and master’s and doctoral degrees; social work and related programmes are also offered at diploma level in some polytechnics and colleges. Awards, accreditation and registration rules are changing, so check your own handbook and the official regulator or professional body for your country.

In England, a social work degree must be approved and includes supervised placements; the title is regulated. In South Africa, the professional Bachelor of Social Work is normally a four-year degree, and registration with the South African Council for Social Service Professions is required to practise. Other countries have their own routes. Always confirm length, fees, placement hours and registration with the official body for the country where you intend to work.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually begins with foundations: what social work is, its history from charity to profession, values and ethics, human growth and development, the person-in-environment and systems perspective, social problems and inequality, psychology for practice, communication and interviewing, and social welfare policy and provision.

Core practice then covers casework with individuals, theories and models for practice, group work, community organisation and development, work with families, child welfare and protection, older people, mental health, health and medical social work, disability and inclusive practice, social work and the law, gender-based violence and trauma-informed practice, field practicum and supervision, research methods, management and administration, and social work in Africa with indigenisation and decolonisation.

Master’s level deepens theory, research and evaluation, social policy analysis and advocacy, and contemporary issues such as migration and climate change. The order can vary, but theory, skills, law and field practice are normally woven together.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study by connecting each idea to a case. After reading a theory, ask what it would lead you to notice, say and do with a family in your area. Write short case notes and a reflective journal. Practise interviewing in pairs, with consent and clear boundaries, and ask for feedback.

Learn the law and policy of the country where you plan to practise, and note the date of every rule. Use the field practicum to test classroom ideas under supervision. Read research critically: distinguish evidence from opinion, and check whether a study can be generalised. Keep a glossary of terms. Where schools of thought disagree, state each view fairly and explain what evidence would support it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include treating social work as only counselling or charity, ignoring structural causes such as poverty and discrimination, and imposing personal or religious values on clients. Students also break confidentiality without a lawful reason, promise more than they can deliver, and fail to record decisions.

Another error is to generalise from one culture or one case to all. Do not cite a law, policy or statistic without checking the current official source. Do not diagnose unless your training and the law allow it. Poor boundaries, missed supervision and late notes harm clients and your professional standing. Finally, do not separate theory from practice: a model you cannot use in a case is not yet learned.

keyPoints: Social work is a regulated profession in many countries and an academic discipline grounded in values, law and evidence.
Human dignity, social justice, self-determination and confidentiality guide practice.
The person-in-environment perspective links individual wellbeing to families, communities and social structures.
Theory must be tested in supervised practice, and practice must be recorded and reviewed.
Always check the current law, policy and registration rules for the country where you work.
Indigenisation asks how social work can be relevant to African contexts without abandoning human rights standards.

en.title: Social Work as a Profession: Definition, Scope and Values
en.short: IFSW definition, differences from charity, counselling and volunteering, core values, fields and national regulation.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text: Social work is a practice-based profession and an academic discipline. The global definition of the International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) says it promotes social change and development, social cohesion, and the empowerment and liberation of people. It draws on social work theories, social sciences, humanities and indigenous knowledge. Its central principles are social justice, human rights, collective responsibility and respect for diversities. Social workers engage people and structures to address life challenges and enhance wellbeing. This makes the work rights-based and structural, not only individual.

sections.heading: Not charity
sections.text: Social work differs from charity, counselling and volunteering. Charity usually gives aid and may not question why need exists. Social work is planned and accountable; it works with people and their environment, and may give material help while assessing, advocating and reviewing. Counselling is a talk-based method for emotional or psychological difficulties. Social workers use counselling skills but also case management, community work and policy practice. Volunteering is unpaid help. Volunteers can assist services, but they are not necessarily social workers. Case: Amina in Kaduna misses school to hawk after her father’s illness. A charity may pay fees; a counsellor may explore distress; a social worker assesses family, school and health, coordinates help, records a plan and advocates with the school.

sections.heading: Values and fields
sections.text: Core values guide practice. IFSW names social justice, human rights, collective responsibility and respect for diversities. Many codes add dignity, relationships, integrity and competence. Main fields include child welfare and protection, health and medical social work, mental health, services for older people, disability, family services, school social work, criminal justice, community development and migration. The field changes tasks, not values.

sections.heading: Bodies and rules
sections.text: Professional bodies and registration differ by country. In the United States, NASW is a membership association; licensing is handled by state boards. In Nigeria, NASOW is the professional association. Requirements to practise, protected titles and regulators vary, so check current national law and the official body before relying on a rule.

keyPoints: The IFSW global definition presents social work as a practice-based profession and academic discipline that promotes social change, cohesion, empowerment and liberation.
Its central principles are social justice, human rights, collective responsibility and respect for diversities.
Social work is planned and accountable, unlike one-way charity, and it is broader than counselling or volunteering.
Social workers may use counselling skills, but they also assess, advocate, coordinate and review plans with people and their environment.
Main fields include child welfare, health, mental health, older people, disability, family services, school social work, criminal justice, community development and migration.

Professional bodies and registration differ by country: NASW in the United States is a membership association, NASOW in Nigeria is the professional association, and students should check current national rules.

en.title: History of Social Work: From Charity to Profession
en.short: From religious charity and the COS to settlements, Richmond, colonial welfare and indigenisation.

sections.heading: Charity and organisation
sections.text: Before professional social work, care for the poor was mainly a religious duty. Churches and charities gave alms, meaning direct relief such as food or money. Critics said careless relief encouraged dependency. The Charity Organisation Society, founded in London in 1869, coordinated charities and investigated each applicant. Its volunteer friendly visitors kept records and gave advice. This approach, called scientific charity, was strict and often moralising, but it introduced case records and organised helping.

sections.heading: Settlements and casework
sections.text: The settlement movement offered another model. Toynbee Hall, founded in Whitechapel, East London, in 1884, brought university graduates to live among the poor. Settlements ran classes and clubs and campaigned for housing and labour reform. Jane Addams co-founded Hull House in Chicago in 1889 and became a leading reformer. Mary Richmond’s Social Diagnosis (1917) set out how to gather social evidence systematically. Her casework approach, meaning individual help, studied family, health, income and neighbourhood before planning help. Settlements stressed social causes; Richmond stressed the individual case.

sections.heading: Colonial welfare and training
sections.text: In British colonies in Africa, welfare departments grew especially from the 1940s. They handled juvenile delinquency, destitution and problems of people moving to towns. Colonial Development and Welfare funds supported some work. Early professional training began in South Africa in the 1920s and later spread to universities elsewhere. Imagine Ama, a clerk in a 1950s welfare office. She must decide whether to give a widow food or help her find work. A professional approach records the case, checks family support and plans with her.

sections.heading: Indigenisation debate
sections.text: The indigenisation debate asks how far African social work should use imported Western models. Critics say early training taught British and American methods that ignored local family systems, beliefs and community decision-making. They call for practice built on local knowledge, such as Ubuntu, a southern African idea of shared humanity. Others warn that local customs can be harmful and that professional standards matter. The debate is unsettled and shapes teaching and service design.

keyPoints: The Charity Organisation Society (London, 1869) coordinated relief and introduced investigation and case records.
The settlement movement, including Toynbee Hall (1884), brought educated residents into poor neighbourhoods and combined service with reform.
Jane Addams co-founded Hull House (Chicago, 1889) and linked social work to social reform.
Mary Richmond’s Social Diagnosis (1917) set out systematic fact-gathering for casework.
British colonial welfare departments in Africa expanded from the 1940s, and professional training began in South Africa in the 1920s before spreading.
The indigenisation debate asks how far African social work should adapt or replace Western models with local knowledge.

en.title: Values, Ethics and the Professional Relationship
en.short: Core values, personal versus professional ethics, boundaries, confidentiality and a simple dilemma framework.

sections.heading: Core values
sections.text: Social work ethics rest on widely taught core values. Dignity and worth of the person means treating every person as valuable, whatever their status or choices. Self-determination means respecting a client’s right to make their own decisions, as far as law and safety allow. Social justice means working against unfair treatment and unequal access to resources. Integrity means being honest, reliable and consistent. Competence means having the knowledge and skills to practise safely, and keeping them current. Associations publish codes, but rules differ by country, so check the current code that governs you.

sections.heading: Personal and professional
sections.text: Personal values come from upbringing, culture, religion and experience. Professional values are the shared standards of the role. They do not erase personal values, but in practice the client’s welfare and the code come first. A worker who believes strongly that a young person should stay in school must not impose that belief. Reflection and supervision help workers notice when a personal view is shaping advice.

sections.heading: Boundaries and confidentiality
sections.text: Professional boundaries are the limits on the worker’s role, contact and use of power. They protect clients from exploitation and keep the relationship focused on agreed goals. Confidentiality means keeping client information private. It is not absolute: workers may share information with consent, or when law or serious risk requires it, and they should explain this early. Respect for culture means learning how a client’s language, family and beliefs shape their choices, without stereotyping. Ask rather than assume.

sections.heading: Dilemma framework
sections.text: Use a simple sequence: identify facts and ethical question; list people affected; check values and code; weigh options and consequences; consult a supervisor; decide, act and record. Case: Ngozi, 24, in Ibadan, wants to leave a course her father arranged and asks her worker not to tell him. Personal values may favour education, but self-determination and confidentiality support Ngozi. The worker explores her reasons, explains confidentiality’s limits and agrees what may be shared. The father is not told without lawful or ethical reason.

keyPoints: Dignity and worth, self-determination, social justice, integrity and competence are core social work values.
Professional values guide the role, while personal values must not be imposed on clients.
Boundaries protect clients by limiting the worker’s role, contact and use of power.
Confidentiality is not absolute; share information only with consent or when law or serious risk requires it.
Respect for culture means asking how a client’s background shapes their choices, not stereotyping.
A dilemma framework: identify facts, stakeholders, values and code, weigh options, consult, decide, act and record.

en.title: Human Growth and Development across the Life Span
en.short: Physical, cognitive, emotional and social development from conception to old age, with Piaget, Erikson, Bowlby, Kohlberg.

sections.heading: Stages across life
sections.text: Development is the pattern of change in physical, cognitive, emotional and social capacities from conception to old age. Physical growth is fastest in infancy and puberty, then stabilises; older age brings gradual declines in strength, senses and reaction time. Cognitive development moves from concrete to abstract thinking. Emotional and social development includes attachment, self-control, identity and relationships. Development is lifelong and shaped by culture, family, health and poverty.

sections.heading: Four theories
sections.text: Four theories guide social work. Piaget described cognitive stages: sensorimotor (birth to 2 years), preoperational (2 to 7), concrete operational (7 to 11) and formal operational (11 onward). Children understand best at their stage, so abstract reasoning may confuse a young child. Erikson described psychosocial tasks: trust in infancy, identity in adolescence, intimacy in young adulthood, generativity in midlife and integrity in old age. Bowlby’s attachment theory says a caregiver is a secure base; early separation can affect later relationships. Kohlberg described moral reasoning moving from obedience and punishment, through social approval and law, to universal principles.

sections.heading: Practice implications
sections.text: Stage shapes assessment and communication. With a preoperational child, use play, drawings and short concrete questions, not abstract interviews. With an adolescent, discuss identity and peer pressure, and explain confidentiality and consent. With an older adult, allow time, check hearing and vision, and avoid patronising speech. A case: Amina, aged 8, is referred for school refusal. At the concrete operational stage she can compare concrete examples, so the worker asks her to draw school and name what happens at the gate. The worker interviews her parents and teacher, because development is shaped by home, school and community.

sections.heading: Limits of stage theory
sections.text: These stage theories are useful guides, not fixed boxes. Piaget, Erikson, Bowlby and Kohlberg built their models largely on Western samples, and later research shows cultural and individual variation. Some children reach milestones earlier or later; moral reasoning and attachment behaviour differ across communities. Use stages to inform questions and expectations, but assess the person in their context.

keyPoints: Development is lifelong and shaped by physical, cognitive, emotional, social and cultural factors.
Piaget’s stages move from sensorimotor and preoperational thinking to concrete and formal operational reasoning.
Erikson’s psychosocial tasks include trust, identity, intimacy, generativity and integrity.
Bowlby’s attachment theory describes the caregiver as a secure base and links early separation to later relationships.
Kohlberg’s moral stages move from punishment and obedience to social approval and universal principles.
Match communication to the person’s stage, and remember that stage theories are based largely on Western samples.

en.title: The Person-in-Environment Perspective: Systems, Ecology and Assessment Tools
en.short: Systems theory, Bronfenbrenner’s ecological model, the life model, ecomaps and genograms.

sections.heading: Person and environment
sections.text: Social work rejects the idea that a person’s problems sit only inside the person. The person-in-environment perspective holds that behaviour and wellbeing arise from the ongoing exchange between a person and their surroundings: family, school, community and policy. It widens assessment beyond individual traits, but if used vaguely it explains nothing in particular. It is a perspective, not one theory.

sections.heading: Systems and ecology
sections.text:
General systems theory, from Ludwig von Bertalanffy, describes a system as parts that interact. A family is a system: a change in one member affects the others. Systems have boundaries, inputs, outputs and feedback, and open systems exchange with their environment.

Urie Bronfenbrenner’s ecological model arranges the environment in layers: microsystem (face-to-face settings such as home or class), mesosystem (links between them), exosystem (settings affecting the person without their participation, such as a parent’s workplace), macrosystem (culture, economy, law) and chronosystem (change over time).

sections.heading: The life model
sections.text: Germain and Gitterman’s life model sees people as adapting to their environment across the life course. It focuses on life transitions, environmental pressures and the fit between person and setting. The worker aims to reduce stress, mobilise supports and improve the fit, not treat the person alone.

sections.heading: Ecomap and genogram
sections.text:
An ecomap puts the person or family in a circle at the centre and shows outside systems as circles, joined by lines for strong, weak or stressful relationships. A genogram is a family tree across at least three generations, with squares for males, circles for females, lines for marriage and divorce, and an X to mark a death. It reveals patterns such as repeated illness or caregiving.

Case: Amina, 14, in Kano, Nigeria, has stopped attending school. Her ecomap shows a strong link to her grandmother, a stressful link to school and a weak link to a clinic. Her genogram shows her mother died young and an aunt raised her. The plan supports the home and school re-entry rather than blaming Amina.

keyPoints: The person-in-environment perspective treats problems as arising from the fit between person and setting, not from the person alone.
General systems theory says that parts of a system interact, so a change in one member affects the others.
Bronfenbrenner’s model has five layers: microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem and chronosystem.
The life model of Germain and Gitterman focuses on life transitions, environmental pressures and person-environment fit.
An ecomap maps the person’s links with outside systems; a genogram maps family history across generations.
Both tools are assessment aids: they organise information and suggest points of intervention, but they do not prove causes.

en.title: Social Problems, Social Structure and Inequality
en.short: Covers social structure, socialisation, stratification, poverty measures and Mills’s sociological imagination.

sections.heading: Structure and socialisation
sections.text: A social problem is a condition that many people see as harmful and needing collective action. Social structure is the patterned way people relate through institutions such as family, school, work and the state. Socialisation is the process by which people learn norms, the shared rules of behaviour, and roles, the expected behaviour attached to a position such as parent or worker. Kinship is a network of family ties by blood, marriage or adoption. It can support people but also create obligations.

sections.heading: Stratification and inequality
sections.text: Stratification is the ranking of groups into layers with unequal access to money, power and respect. Class refers to economic position, often linked to occupation, income and wealth. Gender refers to socially built expectations for men and women, not merely biological sex. Ethnicity is a sense of belonging based on shared culture, language or descent. These categories overlap. Inequality becomes a social problem when it limits life chances, meaning people’s chances of good health, education and income.

sections.heading: Poverty and its measures
sections.text: Poverty is a lack of resources needed for a decent life. Absolute poverty uses a fixed line, often a minimum food and basic needs basket. Relative poverty compares income with the usual standard in a society. Multidimensional measures count deprivations in health, education and living standards. Poverty lines differ by country and year, so check the current official source. Public problems such as unemployment, urbanisation and migration are often felt as private strain.

sections.heading: Case and imagination
sections.text: Amina, a young graduate in Lagos, loses her job when the firm cuts staff. She returns to her rural kinsmen for support. Her trouble is personal, but Mills’s sociological imagination asks us to see the link with national unemployment, housing costs and migration. Personal troubles become public issues when many people face the same structural constraint.

keyPoints: Social structure shapes individual choices through institutions, norms and roles.
Stratification ranks groups unequally by class, gender and ethnicity.
Kinship can be a source of support and of obligation.
Absolute poverty uses a fixed line; relative poverty uses a society’s standard.
Multidimensional poverty counts deprivations in health, education and living standards.
Mills’s sociological imagination links personal troubles to public issues.

en.title: Psychology for Social Work: Personality, Learning and Emotion
en.short: Personality, learning, motivation, stress and defence mechanisms for social work assessment.

sections.heading: Personality lenses
sections.text: Personality is a person’s usual pattern of thinking, feeling and behaving. Psychodynamic theory, from Freud, sees behaviour as shaped by unconscious conflict among the id (wishes), ego (reality) and superego (conscience). It also names defence mechanisms, which protect the ego from anxiety. Trait theory describes stable dimensions; the Big Five are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Humanistic theory, especially Carl Rogers, stresses self-concept and conditions of worth. Social-cognitive theory, especially Albert Bandura, stresses learning from others and self-efficacy, a person’s belief that they can act effectively.

sections.heading: Learning and motivation
sections.text: Learning theory explains how experience changes behaviour. Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with one that already produces a response, as in Pavlov’s dogs. Operant conditioning, from Skinner, holds that reinforcement increases behaviour and punishment reduces it. Social learning adds observation and imitation. Motivation may be intrinsic, done for interest, or extrinsic, done for reward. Maslow’s hierarchy suggests needs range from physiological needs to self-actualization, with safety, belonging and esteem in between, but the order is not fixed for everyone.

sections.heading: Stress and coping
sections.text: Stress is the strain when demands seem greater than resources. Lazarus and Folkman describe stress appraisal: a person judges whether an event is threatening and whether they can cope. Problem-focused coping tackles the cause; emotion-focused coping manages feelings. Defence mechanisms such as denial, projection and rationalisation can reduce anxiety in the short term but distort reality if overused. Know these as basic mental health literacy, not as diagnosis.

sections.heading: Case and assessment
sections.text: Amina, 19, misses classes after failing an examination. A social worker avoids labelling her as lazy. Instead the worker asks about sleep, family pressure, beliefs about failure and previous learning experiences. Trait ideas describe her shyness; social-cognitive ideas show low self-efficacy; psychodynamic ideas notice denial; learning ideas identify avoidance that reduces anxiety. The worker records evidence, explores coping and refers for specialist help if needed.

keyPoints: Personality theories offer different lenses: psychodynamic, trait, humanistic and social-cognitive.
Classical conditioning links stimuli; operant conditioning links behaviour to consequences.
Reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment reduces it.
Stress depends on appraisal, and coping can target the problem or the emotion.
Defence mechanisms reduce anxiety but can distort reality.
Use psychological ideas to understand behaviour and emotion, not to diagnose mental illness.

en.title: Communication and Interviewing Skills in Social Work
en.short: The helping interview: listening, empathy, questions, culture, interpreters, stages and case notes.

sections.heading: Listening and empathy
sections.text: Active listening means giving full attention, noticing words and feelings, and showing that you follow. Empathy is understanding the client’s world from their viewpoint and communicating that understanding without judging. It differs from sympathy, which is feeling sorry for someone. Silence can be useful: it lets the client think or decide whether to continue. Non-verbal communication includes eye contact, posture, tone and gestures. Its meaning varies by culture, so check rather than assume.

sections.heading: Questions and responses
sections.text: Open questions invite description, for example 'What happened next?' Closed questions seek a yes, no or short fact, such as 'Do you sleep at home?' Use closed questions for detail and safety checks, not for the whole interview. Probing follows up gently to get a fuller picture. Paraphrasing restates the main point in your own words to check accuracy. Reflecting feeling names the emotion you hear, such as 'You sound frightened.' Both help the client feel understood.

sections.heading: Culture and stages
sections.text: Cross-cultural communication requires cultural humility: ask about the client’s language, family roles and beliefs, and avoid stereotypes. If language is a barrier, use a trained interpreter, not a child or relative. Speak to the client, not the interpreter, and allow extra time. A helping relationship usually moves through engagement, assessment, intervention and ending. Explain confidentiality and its limits early. Review goals before ending and discuss feelings about closure.

sections.heading: Case notes and example
sections.text: Case notes are written records of contact. Record date, time, people present, facts, decisions and actions. Separate observation from inference: write 'Amina said she had not eaten' rather than 'Amina is neglected'. Quote key words, keep notes confidential and store them securely. Example: Amina says she misses school to care for her mother. The worker asks 'Tell me about a typical day', paraphrases, reflects 'You sound worried', and notes the facts and the agreed next step.

keyPoints: Active listening and empathy show the client that you are trying to understand their world.
Open questions invite description; closed questions confirm facts or safety.
Probing, paraphrasing and reflecting feeling check meaning and deepen the interview.
Silence and non-verbal cues carry meaning, but their meaning varies by culture.
Use a trained interpreter and avoid treating one culture’s customs as universal.
Case notes should be factual, dated, confidential and separate observation from inference.

en.title: Social Welfare Policy and the Organisation of Welfare
en.short: Social policy models, the mixed economy of welfare, social security and services, and how policy shapes practice.

sections.heading: Models of welfare
sections.text: Social policy studies how societies organise welfare: laws, budgets and services that meet needs such as income, health and care. The residual model treats welfare as a safety net for people who fail in the market or whose family cannot help; benefits are often means-tested (based on income) and modest. The institutional model treats welfare as normal, with universal services that prevent hardship. The developmental model links welfare to economic and social development, investing in people’s capabilities. Most countries mix these types. Titmuss described residual and institutional models; Midgley, developmental welfare.

sections.heading: Mixed economy
sections.text: No country provides welfare through the state alone. The mixed economy of welfare, or welfare pluralism, divides provision among four sectors. The state provides statutory services and social security. The market sells private insurance, health care and education. The family gives unpaid care, food and remittances. The voluntary sector includes NGOs, faith groups and community associations. A child protection case may involve a state social worker, an NGO shelter and the extended family. Policy decides who does what and pays.

sections.heading: Social security and services
sections.text: Social security means cash benefits that protect income, such as pensions, child grants and unemployment support. It may be contributory or non-contributory (tax-funded, universal or means-tested). Social services are personal services such as child protection and disability support. For example, a grandmother in Kenya caring for orphans may receive a cash transfer and a social worker’s visit. The cash is social security; the visit is a social service. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and ILO Convention No. 102 (1952) set standards; UNICEF supports child protection systems.

sections.heading: Policy and practice
sections.text: Policy shapes what a social worker can do. Legislation sets duties and eligibility; budgets set staff and places. A social worker may assess for a grant, refer to a service, or advocate for a gap. The UN sets rights standards, UNICEF supports programmes, and the ILO promotes social security. Social workers should check current law and rules in their country.

keyPoints: Social policy studies the laws, budgets and services that organise welfare.
The residual model is a means-tested safety net; the institutional model provides universal services; the developmental model invests in people’s capabilities.
The mixed economy of welfare divides provision among state, market, family and voluntary sector.
Social security provides cash benefits; social services provide personal help such as child protection and disability support.
The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and ILO Convention No. 102 (1952) set international standards, and UNICEF supports child protection systems.
Policy shapes what a social worker can do by setting duties, eligibility and budgets.

en.title: Social Casework: The Helping Process with Individuals
en.short: Referral to termination, Perlman, task-centred work, crisis intervention, involuntary clients, use of self and recording.

sections.heading: The helping process
sections.text: Referral is when a client comes to the agency through another person or agency, or by self-referral, with consent where possible. Intake decides whether the agency fits and whether the client wants help. Assessment gathers facts about the person, the problem, the environment and the client’s strengths. Planning turns these into agreed goals. Intervention is the work itself; monitoring checks progress; evaluation judges whether goals were met. Termination ends the relationship on purpose, reviewing gains and planning for setbacks.

sections.heading: Perlman and task-centred practice
sections.text:
Helen Harris Perlman’s problem-solving model (Social Casework, 1957) organises casework around four Ps: the person, the problem, the place (the agency) and the process. The client’s own definition of the problem is central, and the worker offers a relationship in which it can be tackled.

Task-centred practice, developed by William Reid and Laura Epstein, agrees a few explicit tasks with the client, sets a time limit of roughly six to twelve interviews, and reviews progress. It suits concrete, agreed problems.

sections.heading: Crisis intervention
sections.text: A crisis is a temporary state of upset in which usual coping fails. Crisis intervention is brief and aims to restore functioning, not to rework personality. Gerald Caplan helped develop the theory; Albert Roberts set out a widely used staged model, moving from checking danger and lethality, through rapport and defining the problem, to an action plan and follow-up.

sections.heading: Involuntary clients, self and recording
sections.text:
Involuntary clients come through court order, school or family pressure. The worker names the mandate honestly and looks for any area the client does want to change. Use of self means using one’s own personality, feelings and judgement deliberately, aware of their effect.

Case example: Amina, 15, is referred by her school for repeated absence. Assessment finds she cares for younger siblings while her mother trades. The agreed plan shares the care and links her to a homework club. Recording keeps this accountable: SOAP notes (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) separate fact from opinion.

keyPoints: The helping process runs from referral and intake through assessment, planning, intervention, monitoring and evaluation to termination.
Perlman’s problem-solving model centres casework on the person, problem, place and process.
Task-centred practice sets a few explicit tasks within a short time limit and reviews them.
Crisis intervention is brief and aims to restore functioning rather than change personality.
With involuntary clients, name the mandate honestly and find areas the client does want to change.
Records such as SOAP notes should separate observed fact from professional opinion and are confidential.

en.title: Theories and Models for Social Work Practice: Choosing and Combining Approaches
en.short: Nine practice models, choosing and combining them, evidence, and critical use in African settings.

sections.heading: Main models
sections.text:
Psychodynamic practice links present difficulties to early relationships and unconscious conflict. Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) connects thoughts, feelings and actions and uses structured tasks to test unhelpful thinking. Person-centred practice trusts the client’s capacity to grow and offers empathy, genuineness and unconditional positive regard.

Systems practice treats the person as part of a family or network and works on relationships and feedback loops. The strengths perspective begins with client resources, not deficits. Empowerment practice seeks to reduce powerlessness and increase clients’ control. Solution-focused practice asks about preferred futures and small next steps. Narrative therapy separates people from problem-saturated stories and invites alternative accounts. Motivational interviewing is a collaborative conversation that strengthens a client’s own reasons for change.

sections.heading: Choosing and combining
sections.text:
Choice depends on the client’s needs, risk, culture, age, setting and the worker’s training. Models can be combined when their assumptions fit.

A strengths assessment can sit beside CBT tasks. Do not mix approaches mechanically. Agree a purpose, review progress and change course if the client is not helped. Supervision and client preference guide the decision.

sections.heading: Evidence and context
sections.text:
Evidence-based practice means combining the best research with professional judgement and client values and preferences. It does not mean applying a manual to everyone. Most models were developed in Western countries. Their assumptions about individualism, family authority, religion, language and help-seeking may fit poorly elsewhere.

In African settings, ask whether a model is culturally valid, who defined the problem and what supports exist. Adapt with community input and check outcomes.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text:
Aminu, 16, is referred for fighting at school in Kano, Nigeria. CBT could track triggers and teach anger coping. A systems view includes his uncle, who cares for him, and the school.

A strengths approach notes his football coaching and respect for his uncle. Motivational interviewing explores what Aminu wants to change. The worker combines these after agreeing goals with Aminu and his uncle, then reviews after six weeks.

keyPoints: Models are tools, not identities: choose by client need, risk, culture, setting and worker competence.
CBT is structured and skills-focused; psychodynamic work explores early patterns; person-centred work provides empathy and unconditional positive regard.
Systems, strengths and empowerment models shift attention to relationships, resources and power.
Solution-focused, narrative and motivational interviewing approaches use client language and goals to support change.
Evidence-based practice combines research, professional judgement and client values; it is not rigid manual application.
Western models need cultural adaptation and local validation before use in African settings.

en.title: Social Group Work: Dynamics and Facilitation
en.short: Group types, Tuckman’s stages, roles, norms, cohesion, conflict, facilitation and African self-help groups.

sections.heading: Types of groups
sections.text:
A social group is people who interact, share a purpose and see themselves as a group. Recreational groups offer leisure. Educational groups teach skills or information.

Support groups help members cope with a shared experience, such as HIV or bereavement. Therapeutic groups use guided interaction to heal distress or change behaviour, usually led by a trained worker. Task groups complete a job, such as a committee planning a clinic. The type shapes purpose, leadership and rules.

sections.heading: Stages and dynamics
sections.text:
Tuckman’s stages are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Forming is polite dependence; storming brings disagreement over power and purpose; norming settles shared rules; performing is work on the task; adjourning is ending.

Norms are expected behaviour, often unspoken. Roles are parts members take, such as initiator, harmoniser, blocker or scapegoat. Cohesion is the pull keeping members together; it aids support but can silence dissent. Conflict is normal. Handled openly, it can improve decisions; ignored, it can split the group.

sections.heading: Planning and facilitation
sections.text:
Plan by defining purpose, assessing need, choosing members and size, setting time and venue, agreeing confidentiality and consent, and planning evaluation.

Facilitate with an agenda, ground rules, warm-up, balanced participation, summarising and a closing review. Handle difficult members calmly. For a monopoliser, use round robin (each person speaks in turn) or a private word. For silent members, offer pair work. For hostility, name the behaviour, not the person, and restate the agreement. Protect safety and refer when needs exceed the group.

sections.heading: African self-help groups
sections.text:
In many African communities, self-help groups pool labour, money or care. Savings groups include rotating schemes such as esusu in Nigeria and susu in Ghana, and other local forms such as chama in Kenya and stokvel in South Africa. They offer credit and mutual aid. Support groups for people living with HIV or for widows reduce isolation.

A worker should respect local rules and avoid imposing outside models. Example: in a Lagos savings group, members agree a weekly contribution; when one member cannot pay, the group decides whether to wait or lend from a fund.

keyPoints: Group type shapes purpose, leadership and rules.
Tuckman’s stages are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning.
Norms are shared expectations; roles are the parts members take.
Cohesion supports members but can silence dissent; conflict handled openly can improve decisions.
Plan a group by defining purpose, assessing need, agreeing confidentiality and planning evaluation.
Self-help and savings groups such as esusu, susu, chama and stokvel are common in African communities and should be respected, not replaced.

en.title: Community Organisation and Community Development
en.short: Needs assessment, participatory methods, Rothman’s models, self-help, organiser roles and project evaluation.

sections.heading: Models and roles
sections.text:
Community organisation is the social work process of helping people identify needs, plan and act collectively. Community development is the improvement of social and economic conditions through participation and self-help. Jack Rothman described three models of community organisation practice: locality development, which builds local capacity and cooperation; social planning, which uses expert data and planning; and social action, which organises disadvantaged groups to shift power and resources, often through conflict.

The worker’s role changes. An organiser mobilises people and builds groups. A facilitator enables dialogue and inclusion without deciding for the community. An advocate speaks with or for a group to obtain services, rights or resources.

sections.heading: Assessment and participation
sections.text:
Community needs assessment gathers information about problems, strengths and priorities before action. Methods include surveys, key informant interviews, focus groups and community mapping. Participatory methods involve residents in collecting and analysing information, including participatory rural appraisal (PRA), transect walks, seasonal calendars and ranking. Participation should include women, youth, disabled people and marginalised groups.

Self-help approaches build on local resources: savings groups, cooperatives, mutual aid and volunteer work. External support should strengthen these efforts. For example, in a Nigerian town, a social worker might help a residents’ association map drainage. Residents could rank a blocked channel as the main problem, form a cleanup committee and seek local government support. The worker would facilitate but not lead.

sections.heading: Leaders and evaluation
sections.text:
Local leaders and traditional structures, such as chiefs, elders, religious leaders and women’s associations, can open access and sustain projects. The worker should meet them early, clarify expectations and avoid letting one leader speak for everyone. Traditional authority can exclude residents, so the worker must create separate spaces for marginalised voices.

Evaluation asks whether a project met its aims. It uses indicators agreed before work starts, such as drainage blockages or illness reports. Good evaluation compares before and after, collects numbers and stories, and asks residents to judge results. It reports unintended effects and feeds lessons into the next phase.

keyPoints: Community organisation helps people identify needs and act collectively; community development adds wider social and economic improvement through participation and self-help.
Rothman’s three models of community organisation are locality development, social planning and social action.
The worker may act as organiser, facilitator or advocate, and should not decide for the community.
Needs assessment uses surveys, interviews, focus groups and mapping; participatory methods involve residents in gathering and ranking information.
Work with chiefs, elders and religious leaders early, but protect space for marginalised voices.
Evaluate against agreed indicators, compare before and after, and use findings to adjust the project.

en.title: Social Work with Families
en.short: Family systems, life cycle, genograms, assessment, couple and parenting work, and African kin and polygyny.

sections.heading: Family systems
sections.text:
A family system is a set of members who are interconnected, so a change in one member affects the others. Social workers look at boundaries (who is inside or outside), roles, rules, communication and homeostasis, the system’s tendency to keep its usual pattern. They also think about circular causality: each person’s behaviour both causes and responds to the others. The family life cycle is the sequence of stages and transitions, such as forming a couple, raising young children, launching children and later life. Stress often appears at transitions.

A genogram is a diagram of at least three generations. It records names, ages, marriages, births, deaths, illness, migration and close or cut-off relationships. It helps the worker and family see patterns across time.

sections.heading: Assessment and approaches
sections.text:
Family assessment is the structured gathering of information about structure, roles, communication, strengths, risks, culture, resources and safety. The worker agrees with the family what to explore and records differing views.

Common family approaches include structural work, which aims to clarify or change boundaries and alliances; strategic work, which interrupts repeated problem cycles; solution-focused work, which builds on exceptions and small goals; narrative work, which separates the person from the problem; and behavioural parent training. Couple work helps partners hear each other, manage conflict and repair after arguments. The worker stays neutral but screens each partner alone for violence. Parenting support teaches praise, routines, clear and consistent limits, and age-appropriate expectations.

sections.heading: African family forms
sections.text: Many African families include extended kin, and care may be shared. Polygyny is one man married to more than one woman; its legal and customary status varies by country and religion, so check local law. Kinship care means relatives raise a child. Practice should involve kin with consent, clarify who decides, explain confidentiality limits and keep child safety central. For example, Amina, 14, lives with an aunt and refuses school. The worker maps the genogram, includes aunt and parents, agrees who to consult, and offers parenting support.

keyPoints: A family system is interconnected, so change in one member affects all, and circular causality matters.
The family life cycle highlights transitions as times of stress and adjustment.
A genogram maps at least three generations and reveals patterns across time.
Family assessment balances strengths, risks, culture and safety, not just problems.
Family approaches include structural, strategic, solution-focused, narrative and behavioural parent training.
In African family practice, involve extended kin and kinship carers with consent, clarify decision-making and check local law on polygyny.

en.title: Child Welfare and Child Protection: Rights, Safety and Family
en.short: Abuse types, signs and disclosure, safeguarding, CRC and African Charter, alternative care and rights tensions.
keywords: African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child

sections.heading: Abuse and neglect
sections.text: Child welfare is the broad wellbeing of children. Child protection is the narrower work of preventing and responding to abuse, neglect, exploitation and violence. Physical abuse is non-accidental injury. Sexual abuse is any sexual act or exploitation involving a child. Emotional abuse is persistent rejection, threats or humiliation. Neglect is failure to meet basic needs such as food, health care, supervision and affection. Forms often overlap.

sections.heading: Signs and disclosure
sections.text: Signs are indicators, not proof. They include patterned injuries, poor explanations, fear of home, age-inappropriate sexual knowledge, withdrawal, self-harm, hunger and school absence. When a child discloses, listen calmly, use open questions, do not interrogate and do not promise secrecy. Record exact words, explain next steps and report promptly to the designated safeguarding officer or statutory agency. Case: nine-year-old Chidi in Nigeria tells his teacher an uncle hurts him at night. The teacher records, comforts him and refers the same day; she does not investigate.

sections.heading: Safeguarding process
sections.text: Safeguarding is action to keep children safe and promote wellbeing. A common process is recognise, respond, report, record and review. Recognise signs; respond with immediate safety and calm communication; report to the proper authority; record factual, dated notes; review the plan. Mandatory reporting rules and age limits differ by country, so check local law. Multi-agency work with health, school, police and social services is good practice. The child’s best interests guide decisions, and parents are involved where safe.

sections.heading: Rights, care and tension
sections.text: The Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC, 1989) sets four principles: non-discrimination, best interests, survival and development, and respect for the child’s views. The African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child adds duties and community responsibilities, and prohibits harmful practices and child marriage. Alternative care includes kinship, foster, adoption and residential care; family-based care is preferred, with gatekeeping, meaning careful control over which children enter care. Tension arises when community practice, such as corporal punishment or exploitative fostering, conflicts with child rights. Respect culture, but do not treat it as a defence for harm.

keyPoints: Child protection is the narrower response to abuse, neglect, exploitation and violence; child welfare is the broader wellbeing of children.
Physical, sexual and emotional abuse and neglect often overlap, so assess the whole child.
Signs are indicators, not proof; a disclosure should be listened to calmly, recorded in the child’s words and referred promptly.
Safeguarding follows recognise, respond, report, record and review, with mandatory reporting rules set by national law.

The CRC sets non-discrimination, best interests, survival and development, and respect for the child’s views; the African Charter adds duties and community responsibilities and prohibits harmful practices and child marriage.
Alternative care should be family-based where safe, with gatekeeping; culture matters, but it never justifies harm.

en.title: Social Work with Older People
en.short: Ageing, ageism, dementia, elder abuse, assessment, carers and family support in later life.

sections.heading: Ageing and ageism
sections.text: Ageing is the physical, psychological and social change that comes with time. Chronological age is only a rough guide; functional ability matters more. Ageism is prejudice or discrimination based on age. It appears in jokes, hiring, health care and assumptions that older people cannot learn or decide. Retirement is the formal end of paid work. Its meaning varies by country and job: some people have pensions, many in low-income countries never retire formally and keep working in farming, trade or the informal economy.

sections.heading: Loss, dementia and abuse
sections.text: Bereavement is grief after a death; older people may face repeated losses of spouse, friends and status. Dementia is a syndrome of progressive cognitive decline, such as memory and reasoning problems, and it is not normal ageing. Social workers support dignity, decision-making and carers. Elder abuse is harm to an older person by someone trusted, including physical, psychological, sexual, financial abuse and neglect. Safeguarding means reducing risk while respecting rights.

sections.heading: Assessment and planning
sections.text: Assessment gathers the older person’s wishes, health, mobility, income, housing, relationships and risks. A strengths-based assessment records what the person can do and what support exists. Care planning turns this into agreed, person-centred actions with named people and a review date. Example: Mama Ngozi, 74, in Enugu, Nigeria, has no pension, lives with a grandson and is forgetful. Her son works in Lagos. Assessment finds unpaid bills, carer strain and a treatable infection. The plan links a community clinic, a church group, a neighbour for respite and a family meeting.

sections.heading: Carers and community
sections.text: Carers are relatives or friends who provide unpaid support. They need information, training, counselling, respite (short breaks) and recognition. Where pensions are limited or cover only formal workers, older people often depend on savings, family, remittances and community ties. Extended family and community can provide care and status, but they are not automatic safeguards. Urban migration, small incomes and conflict can weaken support. Social workers should work with customary and faith networks without assuming every family will care well.

keyPoints: Ageing is more than chronology; functional ability and social context shape need.
Ageism is prejudice or discrimination based on age and can affect access to care and work.
Dementia is not normal ageing; social work supports dignity, decision-making and carers under strain.
Elder abuse includes financial, physical, psychological and sexual harm and neglect by trusted people.
Assessment should be holistic, strengths-based and led by the older person’s wishes.
Carers need information, respite and recognition, and extended family support should be worked with rather than assumed.

en.title: Mental Health and Social Work: Recovery, Law and Team Practice
en.short: Mental disorder categories, biopsychosocial model, stigma, recovery, mental health law and team roles.

sections.heading: Categories and model
sections.text: ICD-11 (WHO) and DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association) classify mental disorders into categories: mood, anxiety, psychotic, substance use, trauma-related, neurodevelopmental, personality, eating and neurocognitive disorders. Categories aid communication and treatment, but overlap and change with revision. The biopsychosocial model, proposed by George Engel, explains distress through interacting biological, psychological and social factors. Social workers assess housing, income, family, work, discrimination and safety alongside symptoms.

sections.heading: Stigma and recovery
sections.text: Stigma is a mark of disgrace that leads to exclusion. Public stigma is held by others; self-stigma is internalised; structural stigma is built into laws, services and employment. It delays help-seeking and worsens outcomes. Recovery is not cure. It means building a meaningful life, hope, identity and control with support. Recovery-oriented practice is person-centred, strengths-based and promotes social inclusion. Social workers challenge discriminatory language and help people access work, housing, education and peer support.

sections.heading: Law and involuntary care
sections.text: Mental health law sets when the state may detain or treat someone without consent. It differs by country. For example, Nigeria’s Mental Health Act 2021 and England and Wales’s Mental Health Act 1983 provide procedures, but criteria, review bodies and safeguards vary. Involuntary care should be a last resort, based on defined risk and legal criteria, with independent review, legal representation and the least restrictive option. Social workers contribute statutory assessments only where national law gives them that role. They must know local law and record decisions carefully.

sections.heading: Community and teams
sections.text: Community mental health care supports people outside hospital through teams, outreach, supported housing and psychosocial rehabilitation. It aims to reduce admission and maintain family and community ties. In multidisciplinary teams, psychiatrists, nurses, psychologists, occupational therapists and social workers share tasks. The social worker contributes social assessment, family and community links, safeguarding, benefits and housing advice, advocacy and discharge planning. Example: Amina, 24, in Lagos who hears voices is supported by a community team that respects her family’s beliefs, assesses stigma and housing, and agrees a safety plan.

keyPoints: ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR classify mental disorders, but categories overlap and are revised.
The biopsychosocial model links biological, psychological and social causes of distress.
Stigma can be public, self or structural, and it delays help-seeking.
Recovery means building a meaningful life, not simply removing symptoms.
Mental health law and involuntary care differ by country and require legal safeguards.
In multidisciplinary teams, social workers add social assessment, advocacy and community links.

en.title: Health and Medical Social Work
en.short: Social dimensions of illness, hospital social work, discharge, chronic illness, HIV, palliative care and teamwork.

sections.heading: Illness as social
sections.text:
Health and medical social work addresses the social, emotional and practical sides of illness. A diagnosis affects work, income, housing, family roles and identity, not only the body. Social workers assess these effects, help patients and families understand choices, and link them to benefits, transport, food and counselling.

Hospital social work is short-term and team-based: psychosocial assessment, crisis support, safeguarding and planning for leaving hospital.

sections.heading: Discharge and chronic illness
sections.text:
Discharge planning begins early. It means assessing what the patient needs at home, involving family, and coordinating with doctors, nurses, therapists and community services. Safe discharge may require medication, follow-up appointments, housing, transport or home care. Without this, readmission is more likely.

Chronic illness lasts months or years. Social workers support self-management, family coping, income and school or work adjustments. They also address adherence, meaning whether a person takes treatment as agreed. Adherence depends on social factors: cost, transport, food, disclosure, side effects and trust in staff.

sections.heading: HIV, stigma and palliative care
sections.text:
HIV and AIDS show why medical and social work must join. Stigma, meaning negative labelling, fear of disclosure and discrimination can delay testing and disrupt antiretroviral therapy (ART). Social workers provide confidential counselling, support groups and community education, and challenge discrimination.

Palliative care aims to relieve pain and suffering and improve quality of life for people with serious illness and families. It is not only care at the end of life. Social workers help with advance care planning, family meetings, bereavement support and practical needs.

sections.heading: Teamwork and case
sections.text:
Collaboration with health workers means clear roles, shared plans and confidentiality. In Kenya, community health volunteers (CHVs) are part of primary health care and may support follow-up and adherence.

Case: Amina, 34, in Kano, Nigeria, is admitted with HIV and tuberculosis and fears disclosure. The social worker assesses her safety, explains confidentiality, counsels her on disclosure options, links her to a support group and coordinates with the TB clinic and a community health extension worker for follow-up, transport and food support before discharge.

keyPoints: Health and medical social work addresses the social, emotional and practical effects of illness.
Discharge planning starts early and coordinates the patient, family, health team and community services.
Chronic illness and adherence are shaped by social factors such as cost, transport, stigma and disclosure.
HIV stigma can delay testing and disrupt ART; social workers offer confidential support and challenge discrimination.
Palliative care relieves suffering and improves quality of life, and is not only end-of-life care.
Collaboration with health workers and community health volunteers requires clear roles and confidentiality.

en.title: Disability and Inclusive Practice
en.short: Models of disability, the CRPD, rights-based assessment, independent living and inclusive practice.

sections.heading: Models of disability
sections.text: The medical model treats disability as a problem inside the person, to be diagnosed, treated or cured. The social model, developed by disabled activists and scholars, separates impairment (a body or mind difference) from disability (the barriers society creates). It points to steps, attitudes, communication and rules that exclude people. Most practice uses both: support health needs while removing barriers. The charity model offers pity and gifts; the rights model, expressed in the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD, 2006), treats persons with disabilities as holders of rights who should control their own lives.

sections.heading: Assessment and support
sections.text: Assessment is not only diagnosis. A person-centred assessment asks what the person wants to do, what supports and barriers exist, and what strengths family and community offer. Independent living means having choice and control over daily life, not necessarily living alone; personal assistance and accessible housing can make it possible. Inclusive education means a local school changes to include a disabled learner through ramps, teaching adjustments, sign language or extra time. This is reasonable accommodation: changes that do not impose a disproportionate burden. Work with families is family-centred. Social workers listen to caregivers, offer information and respite, and avoid blaming them.

sections.heading: Case and anti-stigma practice
sections.text: Amina, 14, uses a wheelchair in a Nigerian town. Her school says she cannot enrol because there is no ramp. A social worker assesses the environment, not just Amina. She meets Amina, her parents and the school, agrees a ramp and ground-floor class, and links the family to a disabled persons organisation. She also talks with teachers about assumptions that wheelchair users cannot learn. In African communities, stigma may be framed through curses, shame or witchcraft. Practice should not mock such beliefs. It should discuss them respectfully with families and faith and traditional leaders, share accurate information, and build on community care. Laws and services differ by country, so check current national disability law and local support.

keyPoints: The medical model locates disability in the individual; the social model locates it in barriers.
The CRPD (2006) is a rights treaty based on dignity, participation, equality and accessibility.
Rights-based practice replaces charity and pity with entitlements, choice and control.
Assessment should be person-centred and examine barriers, supports and strengths, not only diagnosis.
Independent living means choice and control with support, not necessarily living alone.
Inclusive education requires reasonable accommodation and changes to the school, not just placing a learner in a class.

en.title: Social Work and the Law: Duties, Evidence and Advocacy
en.short: Child protection, mental health, domestic violence and juvenile justice law, court reports, evidence and advocacy.

sections.heading: Duty and discretion
sections.text: Law gives social workers duties (things they must do) and powers (things they may do). It also leaves discretion: the professional judgement to choose among lawful options. In South Africa, the Children’s Act 38 of 2005 sets child protection duties, while the Mental Health Care Act 17 of 2002 regulates care, treatment and involuntary admission. England and Wales have the Children Act 1989 and Mental Health Act 1983. Discretion is not freedom to ignore the law. Workers must record facts, reasons and decisions, and act within human rights and natural justice.

sections.heading: Four legal areas
sections.text: Child protection law sets duties to investigate harm and protect children; the best interests of the child is a guiding principle in many countries and in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989). Domestic violence law provides protection orders and criminal offences; South Africa’s Domestic Violence Act 116 of 1998 and England and Wales’ Domestic Abuse Act 2021 are examples. Juvenile justice law deals with children who offend, favouring diversion and rehabilitation; South Africa’s Child Justice Act 75 of 2008 is one model. Rules differ by country, so check the current official text.

sections.heading: Court reports and evidence
sections.text: A court report is a written assessment for a court. It should separate fact from opinion, cite sources, state the child’s or adult’s views, and make clear recommendations. Giving evidence means answering questions under oath or affirmation. Prepare, use your records, answer only what is asked, and say when you do not know. Confidentiality can be limited by law or by a court order.

sections.heading: Advocacy and example
sections.text: Advocacy means speaking with or for a person to secure rights or services. Case advocacy concerns one person; policy advocacy concerns rules. Example: a worker must report a child at risk under the Children’s Act 38 of 2005. The law creates the duty; discretion lies in how urgently to act and what support to arrange. The worker records the risk, informs the supervisor and proposes a lawful plan.

keyPoints: Law creates duties and powers, while professional discretion is the lawful judgement to choose among options.
Child protection, mental health, domestic violence and juvenile justice law differ by country; always check the current official text.
Court reports must separate fact from opinion and give clear, evidence-based recommendations.
When giving evidence, prepare, answer only the question asked and state clearly when you do not know.
Advocacy means speaking with or for a person to secure rights and services.
Record the facts and reasons for decisions, because records support accountability and court evidence.

en.title: Gender-Based Violence, Trauma and Trauma-Informed Practice
en.short: Forms and dynamics of gender-based violence, trauma effects, risk assessment, safety planning and prevention.

sections.heading: Forms and dynamics
sections.text:
Gender-based violence (GBV) is violence directed at a person because of gender or unequal power. Forms include physical, sexual, psychological and economic abuse, coercive control, stalking and harmful practices such as child marriage. Intimate partner violence is common, but patterns vary by country.

Dynamics often involve power, control, isolation and blame. A cycle of tension, violence and reconciliation describes some cases, not all. Survivors may face pressure to stay silent.

sections.heading: Trauma and effects
sections.text:
Trauma is the lasting emotional and bodily response to overwhelming events such as violence or sexual assault. Effects include fear, hyperarousal (constant alertness), avoidance, flashbacks, shame, dissociation (feeling detached) and difficulty trusting. Depression, anxiety, sleep problems and physical complaints are common.

Trauma affects memory and behaviour, so survivors may seem angry, numb or inconsistent. These are adaptations to danger, not weakness. Not everyone develops post-traumatic stress disorder.

sections.heading: Practice and risk
sections.text:
Trauma-informed practice assumes many clients have experienced trauma and avoids repeating it. Principles are safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration and empowerment. The worker explains confidentiality and its limits, asks permission, offers choices and avoids blaming. It is a stance, not trauma-specific therapy.

Counselling skills include active listening, validation and calm, direct questions asked privately. Do not force disclosure. Use a locally approved structured risk assessment plus judgement. Check threats to kill, weapons, strangulation, stalking, escalation, suicidal thoughts and children at risk.

Safety planning covers safe exits, documents, money, transport, a code word and emergency contacts. Refer with consent to shelters, health care and legal aid; act without consent only when there is imminent danger and the law allows it. Laws and services differ by country; check current sources.

sections.heading: Case and prevention
sections.text:
Case: Amina, 22-year-old student in Kano, Nigeria, tells a social worker her partner threatens her and controls her money. They agree a safety plan and refer her to a shelter and legal aid.

Community prevention with men and boys uses school, sports and fatherhood programmes and bystander training to challenge norms that excuse violence. Programmes need evaluation and should not blame survivors.

keyPoints: Gender-based violence is rooted in unequal power and takes physical, sexual, psychological and economic forms.
Trauma responses such as hyperarousal, avoidance and dissociation are adaptations to danger, not weakness.
Trauma-informed practice follows safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration and empowerment.
Risk assessment checks immediate danger, including threats to kill, weapons, strangulation, stalking and escalation.
Safety planning and referral to shelters, health care and legal aid should be done with consent unless imminent danger requires otherwise.
Community prevention with men and boys challenges violent norms, but programmes need evaluation and must not blame survivors.

en.title: Field Practicum and Professional Supervision
en.short: Learning contracts, induction, caseload, supervision, reflective practice, recording and competency assessment.

sections.heading: Starting the placement
sections.text: A field practicum is supervised practice in an agency. It is structured by a learning contract, a written agreement between student, school and agency. It states learning goals, tasks, supervision arrangements, boundaries and review dates. Agency induction comes first: policies on confidentiality, safety, consent, recording and who to report to. The student then receives a caseload, the set of cases they carry. It should be manageable and matched to the student’s stage, with complex or high-risk work shared or supervised. Rules differ by country and programme, so check the school handbook and agency policy.

sections.heading: Supervision and reflection
sections.text: Supervision is regular, planned support and accountability. Individual supervision focuses on the student’s cases, decisions, feelings and learning. Group supervision uses peer feedback and shared themes, but confidentiality must be protected. Reflective practice means thinking carefully about what happened, why, and what to do differently. A reflective journal or critical incident review can support it. The field instructor, also called field educator or practice supervisor, links school and agency. They teach, model professional conduct, observe work, give feedback and assess progress. They also hold power as gatekeepers to the profession.

sections.heading: Recording, conduct and assessment
sections.text: Recording means keeping accurate, factual and timely case notes and reports, stored securely. Professional conduct covers boundaries, confidentiality, consent, punctuality, use of phones and social media, and non-discrimination. Assessment is against the school’s practice competencies, not only good intentions. Evidence may include direct observation, supervision records, a portfolio, reflective writing and agency feedback. Example: Amina, a Nigerian undergraduate, is placed at a community advice centre. Her contract sets three learning goals. She carries four family cases, records each contact and attends weekly individual and fortnightly group supervision. Her field instructor observes one interview, and the midpoint review identifies risk assessment as a gap. She addresses it in a reflective log and final portfolio. The school decides pass or fail using its published criteria.

keyPoints: A learning contract sets goals, tasks, supervision arrangements and review dates for the placement.
Induction should cover agency policies, confidentiality, safety and reporting lines before caseload work begins.
Individual supervision focuses on cases and decisions, while group supervision adds peer learning and must protect confidentiality.
Reflective practice turns experience into learning by asking what happened, why, and what to change.
The field instructor teaches, models conduct, gives feedback and assesses against practice competencies.
Recording and professional conduct are assessed: notes must be factual, timely and secure, and boundaries maintained.

en.title: Research Methods in Social Work
en.short: Problem formulation, designs, sampling, measurement, interviews, ethics and basic analysis for social work research.

sections.heading: Framing the study
sections.text: Research starts with a problem question, not a topic. Problem formulation turns a broad concern, such as school dropout in a named district, into a clear question: what is the relationship between household income and dropout among secondary school pupils there? A good question is answerable, focused and ethically possible. The literature review then maps what is already known, identifies gaps and sharpens concepts. It compares studies, methods and findings, and shows why your question matters. Critical reading asks whether the evidence supports the authors’ claims.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text: Quantitative designs measure variables as numbers and test relationships, often by survey or experiment. Qualitative designs explore meaning and experience through interviews, observation or documents. Mixed methods combine both. Sampling is choosing whom or what to study. Probability sampling, such as simple random sampling, lets you estimate how far results may generalise. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive sampling, is common in qualitative work but limits generalisation. State the population, sampling frame (the list from which the sample is drawn) and sample size, and explain your choice.

sections.heading: Measuring and asking
sections.text: Measurement assigns numbers or categories to observations using clear rules. A questionnaire is a written set of questions; an interview is a spoken exchange, often semi-structured. Both need pilot testing. Avoid leading questions, double-barrelled questions and unclear terms. Check reliability (consistency) and validity (whether you measure the intended concept). For example, a depression scale used in a new language needs translation and testing before use.

sections.heading: Ethics and analysis
sections.text: All research with people needs informed consent, privacy, confidentiality and protection from harm; vulnerable groups need extra care. Vulnerable groups include children, people with disabilities and those in crisis. Most institutions require ethics approval. Basic analysis begins with cleaning data. For numbers, use frequencies, percentages, means and cross-tabulations. For interviews, use thematic analysis: code text, group codes into themes and check them against the data. In a small survey of 40 carers, if 12 report unmet respite needs (short breaks from caring), that is 12 ÷ 40 × 100 = 30 per cent. Report the denominator and do not overclaim from a small non-random sample.

keyPoints: A research question should be focused, answerable and ethical; problem formulation and literature review shape it.
Quantitative designs count and test; qualitative designs explore meaning; mixed methods combine both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling, such as purposive sampling, limits it.
Reliability is consistency; validity is whether the measure captures the intended concept.
Ethics applies to all research: informed consent, confidentiality, protection from harm and approval, with extra care for vulnerable people.
Percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100; mean = sum of values ÷ number of values; report denominators and limits.

en.title: Social Work Management and Administration
en.short: Covers structure, planning, budgeting, staffing, supervision, monitoring and accountability in social services.

sections.heading: Administration and structure
sections.text: Social work administration is the management of people, money, information and systems so that social services are delivered. Direct practice is the face-to-face work of assessment, counselling and support with service users. Administration supports, not replaces, direct practice. An organisational structure is the pattern of roles, authority and coordination in an agency. A small NGO (non-governmental organisation) may have a flat structure, with a coordinator and a few staff. A government welfare department is usually hierarchical, with units for casework, finance and records. Structure should fit the agency’s purpose and size.

sections.heading: Planning and budgeting
