sections.text: Planning sets goals, activities, resources, time and indicators. A budget is a financial plan that estimates income and expenditure for a period. Managers compare actual spending with the budget and explain differences. Case: a youth counselling NGO plans income of 600,000 units. Staff cost 360,000, rent 90,000 and activities 120,000. Total spending is 570,000, leaving a surplus of 30,000. If staff cost rises to 400,000, total spending becomes 610,000, a deficit of 10,000. The manager must revise the plan, raise income or cut costs.

sections.heading: People and supervision
sections.text: Human resource management covers recruitment, job descriptions, deployment, training, support and fair treatment of staff and volunteers. Supervision in management means regular oversight: agreeing tasks, giving support, checking quality and holding staff accountable. It differs from direct practice because the focus is on the worker’s performance and the agency’s duties, not on the service user’s treatment. Good supervision also protects service users and reduces burnout.

sections.heading: Monitoring and accountability
sections.text: Monitoring tracks activities and outputs regularly, such as clients seen. Evaluation judges whether outcomes and impact were achieved. An indicator is a measurable sign of change. Accountability runs upward to funders, boards and regulators, downward to service users, and inward to the agency’s own rules. NGOs depend on donors and boards, so they must report clearly. Government welfare departments use public funds and face civil service rules and political oversight. Both need records, complaints systems and honest reports.

keyPoints: Administration manages resources and systems; direct practice works face to face with service users.
Organisational structure divides roles and authority, and should fit the agency’s size and purpose.
A budget estimates income and expenditure; surplus or deficit = income − expenditure.
Human resource management recruits, supports and deploys staff; management supervision checks performance and accountability.
Monitoring tracks activities and outputs; evaluation judges outcomes and impact.
Accountability runs upward to funders and regulators, downward to service users, and inward to the agency.

en.title: Social Work in Africa: Indigenisation and Decolonisation
en.short: Colonial roots, indigenisation and decolonisation, ubuntu, communal care and culturally grounded practice.

sections.heading: Colonial roots
sections.text:
Social work in many African countries grew from colonial welfare services, missionary charity and Western casework. Early services often focused on individuals and treated local families and communities as deficient. Mission schools and colonial administrations often set the first welfare rules.

After independence, laws, curricula and agencies still carried imported assumptions. The pattern differs by country, so check national histories and professional bodies.

sections.heading: Indigenisation and decolonisation
sections.text:
Indigenisation adapts methods, values and examples to local culture and problems. Decolonisation asks deeper questions about whose knowledge counts, who teaches and how power shapes practice. They overlap but are not the same.

Adding local cases is indigenisation; changing curricula, research and authority is decolonisation. This matters because practice can look local while still controlled by outside standards.

sections.heading: Ubuntu and communal care
sections.text:
Ubuntu is a Nguni term for a relational ethic: a person is formed through relationships with others. It supports communal care, mutual obligation and restorative responses. It is not one policy, and meanings differ across communities.

Use it to guide listening and family involvement, not to assume that every African community is identical. In practice, ubuntu can support mediation and shared responsibility for children or older people.

sections.heading: Culturally grounded methods
sections.text:
Practitioners may work with families, elders, religious bodies and traditional healers. Collaboration needs consent, respect, clear boundaries and referral when medical care is needed. Regulation of healers varies by country.

Case: in a Kenyan town, a social worker planning support for a child learns that an aunt and a church group already share care. She maps the network, agrees roles and keeps a school link rather than replacing it. The worker records the plan and reviews it with the family, because local knowledge and professional duty must both be respected.

keyPoints: Colonial welfare and Western casework shaped social work in many African countries.
Indigenisation adapts practice to local culture; decolonisation questions knowledge and power.
Ubuntu is a relational ethic of personhood through community, not a uniform policy.
Culturally grounded practice works with families, faith groups and traditional healers with consent and boundaries.
Local law and professional codes on traditional healing vary, so check current sources.
Building locally relevant practice means testing imported models against local evidence and values.

en.title: Advanced Social Work Theory: Critical and Contemporary Perspectives
en.short: Critical, feminist, anti-oppressive, structural, postmodern and strengths theory, plus power and reflexivity.

sections.heading: Critical and structural theory
sections.text: Critical social work asks whose interests a theory or service serves. It draws on Marx to argue that poverty and distress are produced by economic arrangements, not personal failure. Radical social work in 1970s Britain (Bailey and Brake) and structural social work in Canada (Mullaly) hold that casework which only adjusts the individual leaves the cause untouched. The task becomes to connect private trouble to public issue (C. Wright Mills) and act on both.

sections.heading: Feminist and anti-oppressive practice
sections.text: Feminist social work (Dominelli and McLeod) treats gender as a structuring relation of power, not a personal attribute. It asks who does the caring, who is assumed to be the problem, and whether the service reproduces women’s dependence. Anti-oppressive practice widens the analysis to race, class, disability, sexuality and age, and insists the worker also holds power in the relationship. Empowerment here means shifting real control over decisions to the person, not merely raising confidence.

sections.heading: Postmodern and strengths approaches
sections.text: Postmodern and constructionist work (Foucault; Berger and Luckmann) treats categories such as truant or neglectful mother as made in language and institutional practice, not found in nature. Foucault’s power/knowledge means that being assessed, recorded and classified is itself an exercise of power. The strengths perspective (Saleebey) answers the deficit habit of assessment by starting from what a person and their network can already do. Critics warn it can become optimism that ignores material constraint.

sections.heading: One referral, four readings
sections.text: Chidi, 15, in a Nigerian city, has missed school for a term. A structural reading points to fees, transport costs and a mother working long hours. A feminist reading asks why care of younger siblings fell to his sister. A strengths reading lists the church network and his repair skills. A constructionist reading asks who decided that truancy was the problem, and what the school’s records leave out. Reflexivity, the worker’s disciplined attention to their own position and effect, stops these readings hardening into dogma.

keyPoints: Critical and structural theory locate the cause of private troubles in social and economic arrangements, not in the individual.
Feminist social work treats gender as a power relation and asks who carries the caring.
Anti-oppressive practice analyses several oppressions at once and includes the worker’s own power.
Postmodern and constructionist theory treats social work categories as made in language and institutional practice.
The strengths perspective starts from existing capacities, but critics say it can underplay material constraint.
Reflexivity means the worker examines their own position and effect on the situation, not only the client’s.

en.title: Advanced Research and Programme Evaluation
en.short: Advanced dissertation and evaluation designs, mixed methods, validity, reviews, analysis, ethics and reporting.

sections.heading: Design choices
sections.text: Mixed methods combine numerical and narrative evidence. A convergent design collects both at the same time and compares them; an explanatory sequential design first measures an outcome, then interviews people to explain it. State the question, the unit of analysis (the level studied, such as person, family or agency) and the comparison group before data collection. In a dissertation proposal, link each question to a method, a timetable and a plan for analysis.

sections.heading: Validity and bias
sections.text: Internal validity asks whether a change really comes from the programme rather than history, maturation or selection. External validity asks whether findings travel to other settings. Bias is systematic error, not random noise. Common sources are sampling, recall, interviewer and social-desirability bias. Triangulation (using more than one source or method), piloting and independent coding reduce it. A systematic review states a clear question, searches several databases, applies inclusion criteria, assesses study quality and synthesises findings transparently.

sections.heading: Evaluation and analysis
sections.text: Evaluation designs include needs assessment, process evaluation, outcome evaluation and impact evaluation. A process evaluation checks whether the programme was delivered as planned. An impact evaluation estimates change attributable to it. For qualitative data, thematic analysis codes transcripts, groups codes into themes and keeps an audit trail. In a simple impact example, an intervention group improves by 8 points and a comparison group by 5; with pooled standard deviation 6, effect size = (8 − 5) ÷ 6 = 0.5. This is often called a moderate standardised difference, but it does not by itself prove causation.

sections.heading: Ethics and audience
sections.text: Ethics approval requires informed consent, confidentiality, protection from harm and fair selection. For vulnerable participants, add assent, referral pathways and secure storage. Present findings to agencies and policymakers in plain language: one page of key messages, a short methods note, tables and clear limits. Avoid overclaiming. A useful report says what was done, what was found, what it means and what should happen next.

keyPoints: Mixed methods combine numerical and narrative evidence to answer one question from more than one angle.
Internal validity concerns whether a change comes from the programme; external validity concerns whether findings travel.
Bias is systematic error, and triangulation, piloting and independent coding help reduce it.
A systematic review uses a clear question, several databases, inclusion criteria and quality appraisal.
Effect size = (mean intervention − mean comparison) ÷ pooled standard deviation; in the example (8 − 5) ÷ 6 = 0.5.
Ethics approval and plain-language reporting to agencies are part of the research, not an afterthought.

en.title: Social Policy Analysis and Advocacy
en.short: Frameworks for policy analysis, stakeholder and cost analysis, advocacy, lobbying and the social worker as policy actor.

sections.heading: Frameworks for analysis
sections.text: Policy analysis asks who makes policy, within what rules, how it is delivered and what it produces. A simple framework separates actors (state, civil society, donors, service users), institutions (laws, budgets, organisational routines), implementation (frontline discretion and capacity) and outcomes (intended and unintended effects). Stakeholder analysis maps groups by power and interest, so a high-power, high-interest group is managed closely and a low-power, high-interest group is kept informed.

sections.heading: Costing and stakeholders
sections.text: Costing turns a proposal into quantities. Estimate the unit cost, multiply by the number of beneficiaries and the periods, then add administrative and delivery costs. Suppose a fictional Nigerian state plans a cash transfer of 10,000 naira a month to 2,000 households for one year. Transfers cost 2,000 × 10,000 × 12 = 240,000,000 naira. Administration at 15 per cent adds 36,000,000, so the total is 276,000,000 naira, or 138,000 naira per household per year. Sensitivity analysis repeats the sum with different assumptions, such as higher costs.

sections.heading: Advocacy and lobbying
sections.text: Advocacy is organised action to change policy, public opinion or practice for a cause or group. Lobbying is narrower: direct contact with legislators or officials about a specific decision. Social workers act as policy actors when they use case evidence, coalitions, media and testimony. As street-level workers they also shape policy through discretion, an idea called street-level bureaucracy. Ethical advocacy obtains consent, represents service users fairly and declares conflicts of interest.

sections.heading: African case example
sections.text: Consider a fictional welfare reform in a Nigerian state: a food subsidy is replaced by a cash transfer. A social worker finds that many rural women lack bank accounts. Stakeholder analysis shows traders fear lost sales, civil society supports the transfer and officials worry about cost. A coalition proposes mobile-money payment, a grievance desk and a phased pilot. The costing includes transaction fees. The reform is amended and piloted. The lesson is that analysis and advocacy can improve design without pretending that evidence settles every political choice.

keyPoints: Policy analysis examines actors, institutions, implementation and outcomes.
Stakeholder analysis ranks groups by power and interest to plan engagement.
Total programme cost = unit cost × beneficiaries × periods + administrative and delivery costs.
Advocacy seeks broad policy change; lobbying is direct contact with decision makers.
Social workers are policy actors through evidence, advocacy and frontline discretion.
Costing and stakeholder analysis make advocacy more credible but do not remove political choices.

en.title: Migration, Climate Change and Social Work
en.short: Displacement, refugees, climate disasters, urbanisation, trauma, family separation and humanitarian coordination.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.text: Displacement is forced movement from home. A refugee is outside their country and unable or unwilling to return because of a well-founded fear of persecution, as defined in the 1951 Convention and, in Africa, widened by the 1969 OAU Convention to include aggression, occupation or events seriously disturbing public order. An internally displaced person (IDP) has not crossed a border, so refugee law does not cover them. People moved mainly by drought, floods or storms are often called environmental migrants or disaster-displaced persons; climate change is not itself a refugee ground in law. Internal migration is movement within a country, and urbanisation is the rising share of people in towns. African examples include drought in the Horn of Africa, flooding in West Africa and displacement in the Lake Chad region.

sections.heading: Social work roles
sections.text: Social workers in humanitarian response assess needs, give psychological first aid, manage cases, safeguard children and vulnerable adults, trace separated families and refer people to health, shelter, legal and food services. They also advocate for affected people and help design resettlement or durable solutions: voluntary return, local integration or third-country resettlement. Practice should be trauma-informed: distress is common, but not everyone is traumatised, and local healing practices matter. Coordination is essential. Social workers share information ethically with government, UN agencies, NGOs, Red Cross or Red Crescent societies and community groups, avoiding duplication and gaps.

sections.heading: Tensions and case
sections.text: Host communities can feel strained by new arrivals, especially over water, housing, jobs and school places. Tensions may include discrimination, language barriers and unequal aid. Family separation raises safeguarding and best-interests questions; rushed adoption is harmful. Case: after floods in a West African town, Amina, 14, is separated from her mother. A social worker registers her, gives psychological first aid, starts tracing through child protection and Red Cross or Red Crescent partners, and places her with a vetted relative. The worker also meets the host family and school to reduce tension and keep Amina in class.

keyPoints: Displacement is forced movement; refugees cross borders, while IDPs do not.
The 1969 OAU Convention widens refugee protection in Africa beyond the 1951 Convention.
Climate-related displacement is usually not a refugee ground in law.
Social workers provide psychosocial support, family tracing, safeguarding and referrals in humanitarian response.
Durable solutions are voluntary return, local integration and third-country resettlement.
Coordination with agencies and host communities reduces gaps and tensions.
